strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: reusing historically resolved, verified issues as inference-time guidance for repository-level repair, avoiding fine-tuning and forward search.

Comprehensive evaluation across three backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3) with a fixed scaffold (Agentless), statistical significance testing (McNemar's test), and difficulty-stratified analysis showing gains are not confined to easy issues.

Multiple ablations: Exemplar Guardian filtering (+2.3 to +5.6%), Guardian run-to-run stability (90% Agree@3), exemplar-rank sensitivity (Top-1 vs Top-3), and a controlled MCTS forward-search comparison with reported token/call overhead (Appendix B, Table 5).
Honest limitations section covering benchmark scope (Python-only), reliance on historical fixes, and dependence on LLM-judge reliability.

Temporal-leakage prevention in exemplar retrieval (only issues resolved strictly before the target issue's creation time), and a thoughtful description of how the method could port to agentic scaffolds like SWE-agent (Appendix C).
weaknesses: Missing the decisive ablation for the central claim. The core contribution is 'backward reasoning distillation' from verified patches, but the paper never compares the distilled plan against simply injecting the raw exemplar (issue description + verified patch/diff) as a few-shot demonstration. Without this, it is impossible to tell whether gains come from the backward distillation procedure or merely from showing the model any worked example of a similar fix. The EG ablation (filtering vs. no filtering) does not answer this.

The formal contribution is thin. Equation P(t_i|t_<i) → P(t_i|t_<i, x, y_k, guidance) describes ordinary prompt conditioning, i.e., retrieval-augmented prompting with a synthesized rationale. Closely related prior work (retrospective/reverse-engineered reasoning [38], CrossFix [36], retrieval-based repair [19], memory-based repair [26]) is acknowledged but the delta over these is not crisply established empirically.

The claimed mechanism is only partially supported. The paper attributes gains to steering localization, but on GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3 localization improvements are marginal while Pass@1 rises ~10%, so the causal story for the majority of the gains is unexplained. The 'replaces costly forward exploration' claim rests on a comparison against the authors' own small MCTS variant, which underperforms even the Agentless baseline by 6 points, suggesting a weak strawman; the authors themselves concede a matched-budget comparison is left to future work.

Serious presentation defects indicating a rushed or unpolished submission: Figure 1 contains leftover internal notes in Chinese (e.g., 'Historical dataset怎么来的？', '不需要分数s，迷惑', 'Stage 3 突出创新点？'), and the method name is inconsistent ('O-CRD' in the text vs. 'ConRAD' in Figure 2, Appendix A.2, and figure labels). These are directly visible flaws in the camera-ready-quality artifact.

Baseline comparability concerns: GPT-4o baseline numbers are copied from prior papers evaluated under potentially different harnesses/versions, and the GPT-5 Agentless baseline (29.7%) sits below MoatlessTools with GPT-4o, raising questions about configuration choices. The transferability score s∈[-1,1] is described as 'recorded for analysis and downstream control' but no analysis of it is ever reported.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, the detailed prompts for the Guardian and three-stage distillation are not provided, and LLM-judge components use the same model as the repair pipeline without self-preference controls.

Potential contamination is not discussed: the exemplar pool is drawn from the same public repositories as SWE-Bench Lite, and GPT-4o/GPT-5 may have memorized the historical fixes during pretraining, meaning 'distilled guidance' could partially resurface memorized patches rather than transfer procedural reasoning.

strengths: The core idea — reusing verified historical fixes as backward-conditioned, procedural in-context guidance rather than forward search — is sensible and clearly motivated, and it is evaluated across three base LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3) rather than a single backbone.

The Exemplar Guardian filtering stage is a reasonable safeguard against negative transfer, and the paper provides an ablation (Table 2), a run-to-run stability analysis (Table 3), and a sensitivity analysis over exemplar rank (Table 4), which is more self-examination than many similar system papers provide.

The MCTS-vs-BRD comparison (Table 4, Table 5) attempts to quantify the cost-effectiveness claim, and the appendix reports the search budget and token/call overhead, partially addressing the 'cheaper than search' claim.
The limitations section is honest about evaluation scope (Python-only SWE-Bench Lite), dependence on historical fix availability, and reliance on LLM-generated judgments.
Temporal filtering of exemplars (only fixes resolved before the target issue's creation time) is a thoughtful anti-leakage design choice that many retrieval-augmented repair papers omit.
weaknesses: The manuscript is visibly unpolished, which undermines confidence in the rest of the work: Figure 1 contains leftover Chinese editorial annotations ('历史 dataset怎么来的？', '不需要分数s，迷惑', 'Stage 3 突出创新点？'), the method is inconsistently named O-CRD / ConRAD / BRD across sections, Figure 2 axis labels say 'ConRAD', and Appendix B references 'Table 5' for content that is actually in Table 4. These are signs the paper was not carefully checked before submission.

The formal contribution in Section 3.3 is thin: the 'BRD formulation' reduces to conditioning next-token prediction on (x, y_k, guidance), i.e., standard prompting with the ground-truth patch in context. Presenting autoregressive conditioning as a novel objective overstates the technical depth; the real method is a multi-stage prompting pipeline.

The central claim that outcome-conditioned reuse 'can replace costly forward exploration' rests on a self-implemented MCTS baseline that underperforms even vanilla Agentless (28.0% vs 34.0% in Table 4), strongly suggesting a strawman configuration. The paper itself concedes in Appendix B that a matched-budget comparison was not performed, yet the abstract and introduction make a system-level claim against forward exploration.

The reported gains (e.g., +10.4 Pass@1 for GPT-4o, +10.3 for GPT-5) are large for what is essentially few-shot prompting with distilled exemplar plans, and the paper does not sufficiently control for confounds: single-run results despite closed-model non-determinism, baseline numbers copied from prior papers evaluated at different times under potentially different API versions and harness settings, and no discussion of GPT-5/DeepSeek training-data contamination for SWE-Bench Lite's well-known public patches.

The ablation setup is confusing and internally inconsistent: Tables 4's numbers (BRD 41.0, Agentless 34.0 on 100 samples) are not directly comparable to Table 1's full-set results (37.7, 27.3), and the text does not clearly reconcile them. The McNemar tests are applied across these mixed settings without clarification.

Key design elements are asserted but not validated: the transferability score s is 'recorded for downstream control' but never used in any experiment; the 'Misleading' label is defined circularly (similar on the surface but 'likely to induce negative transfer') with only 9/100 instances and no human validation of Guardian labels; the Guardian's five-dimension rubric is never shown or evaluated against ground truth.

Reproducibility is weak: no prompts, few-shot templates, decoding parameters, or code/artifact release are provided; the distilled plans themselves (the core artifact) are never shown even as an example, so a reader cannot assess what the 'reasoning plans' actually contain or whether they are merely paraphrases of the exemplar's diff.

The related work positioning overstates novelty: retrieval of similar historical patches/issues for APR is well established (e.g., CrossFix [36], shaping repair space with existing patches [12], memory-based methods [26]); the paper's differentiation from these is by assertion rather than experimental comparison against any retrieval-of-historical-fixes baseline.

Coverage of the method is incomplete: exemplars are accepted for only 195/300 GPT-4o issues (Table 2), yet the paper does not report results conditioned on exemplar availability (with vs. without an exemplar) or describe the fallback behavior, obscuring where the gains actually come from.

strengths: The core idea—reconstructing stage-wise repair guidance backward from verified patches and reusing it as inference-time context—is a sensible and clearly motivated alternative to expensive forward exploration, and it is well positioned relative to prior retrieval-based and MCTS-based work in Section 2.

Consistent empirical gains across three backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3) on SWE-Bench Lite, with statistical testing (McNemar's test) against the direct scaffold, plus a difficulty-stratified analysis covering both Easy and Med-High issues.

The paper includes several useful ablations: the Exemplar Guardian filter (+2.3 to +5.6 Pass@1), a Guardian stability analysis (90% Agree@3 across three runs), exemplar-rank sensitivity (Top-1 vs Top-3 vs no-retrieval), and a controlled MCTS-style comparison with reported call/token overheads (Table 5).

Honest limitations section identifying the Python-only scope, dependence on repositories with sufficient fix history, and reliance on LLM-generated judgments; temporal-leakage prevention (exemplars strictly earlier than the target issue) is described.
weaknesses: A decisive ablation is missing: the paper never compares against the simplest baseline of injecting the retrieved exemplar's raw issue + verified patch (or a naive forward-generated rationale) as a few-shot example. Without this, the central claim that backward/outcome-conditioned distillation (BRD) is what drives the gains is not supported; the evidence only shows that exemplar-guided prompting plus filtering helps.

The MCTS comparison, used for the headline '+13.0% Pass@1 with 9.71x fewer calls' claim, is a self-implemented baseline on 100 samples that underperforms even the Agentless scaffold (28.0% vs 34.0%, Table 4). A forward-search baseline this weak suggests a strawman; the authors acknowledge in Appendix B that a matched-budget comparison is deferred to future work, yet the abstract and intro present this as a main result.

Baseline numbers in Table 1 are taken from prior papers rather than rerun under a unified setup (only Agentless is rerun for GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3), which raises comparability concerns given differing scaffolds, prompts, and evaluation dates; O-CRD's own inference cost (calls/tokens, including Guardian and distillation overhead) is never reported.

The formalism oversells the method: the 'reformulation' P_theta(t_i | t_<i) -> P_theta(t_i | t_<i, x, y_k, guidance) is simply prompting with the patch in context; there is no training, decoding change, or objective modification, so the mathematical framing adds little and the 'distillation' terminology is misleading (no student model or parameter update).

Serious presentation lapses: Figure 1 contains leftover internal editing notes in Chinese ('Historical dataset怎么来的？', '不需要分数s，迷惑', 'Stage 3 突出创新点？'), and the framework is inconsistently named throughout (O-CRD vs 'ConRAD' in Figure 2 and Appendix A.2; 'BRD' vs 'Reverse-Engineered Reasoning Distillation' in the appendix), suggesting a rushed, unpolished manuscript.

Unclear handling and accounting of rejected exemplars: Table 2 shows only 195/300 (GPT-4o) issues receive an exemplar, but the paper does not explain what happens on the remaining issues (presumably fallback to Agentless), which complicates interpretation of the aggregate improvement; per-stage attribution of gains (localization vs patch synthesis) is not decomposed.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is mentioned, the structured prompts/rubrics that drive retrieval, Guardian filtering, and plan distillation are only sketched, and key ablation results on 100-sample subsets (Table 4) lack confidence intervals.

strengths: The core idea — reconstructing repair reasoning backward from verified historical fixes (outcome-conditioned distillation) rather than forward exploration — is well-motivated and clearly differentiated from retrieval-based and memory-based prior work; the distinction between 'retrospectively valid' plans and 'historical fidelity' is a thoughtful framing.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three LLM backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3) on SWE-Bench Lite, statistical significance via McNemar's test, difficulty-stratified analysis, an overlap analysis showing 10 uniquely resolved issues, and a scaffold-generalization experiment on mini-SWE-agent (+10.0 on a 100-issue subset) supporting the scaffold-agnostic claim.

The ablations target the right questions: the Exemplar Guardian ablation shows consistent gains from filtering across all three models, the BRD-vs-MCTS comparison controls the reasoning budget and reports concrete cost ratios (9.71x calls, 2.47x tokens), and the 'Exemplar & Patch (no plan)' variant isolates the contribution of distilled reasoning rather than mere exemplar injection.

Temporal leakage is explicitly addressed (exemplars restricted to issues resolved strictly before the target issue's creation time), and implementation details plus full prompt templates are provided in appendices, supporting reproducibility; code is stated to be publicly available.

The limitations section is honest and specific (Python-only benchmark, dependence on bug-fix history availability, reliance on LLM-generated judgments), and the impact statement appropriately cautions against unvalidated automated patches.
weaknesses: Figure 1 contains leftover draft annotations in Chinese ('Historical dataset怎么来的？', '不需要分数s，迷惑', 'Stage 3 突出创新点？', 'Finalization!!!'), indicating the manuscript was not carefully proofread before submission; this undermines presentation quality and reviewer confidence in overall polish.

The theoretical framing in Section 3.3 is thin: the 'reformulation' Pθ(ti|t<i) → Pθ(ti|t<i, x, yk, guidance) simply restates that the plan is generated by prompting the LLM with the ground-truth fix in context. Presenting this as a formal objective overstates the technical depth of what is a prompt-engineering pipeline.

Table 5 is internally confusing: ConRAD (BRD) is 41.0 while ConRAD (Top-1) is 45.0 on what appear to be the same 100-sample setting, but the relationship between these variants is never explained — Top-1 should presumably equal BRD under full ConRAD. This inconsistency makes the similarity-sensitivity ablation hard to interpret.

The MCTS comparison is against a custom, self-implemented forward-search baseline with a fixed budget (B=3, R=20 rollouts), not a published, tuned system such as SWE-Search; the authors acknowledge this in Appendix F but the abstract-level claim of '9.71x fewer LLM calls' may not generalize to production MCTS-APR systems.

Evaluation is confined to SWE-Bench Lite (300 Python-only issues); the main results were obtained with a single attempt per issue and no variance reporting over repeated runs (only the Guardian, on a 100-sample subset, has stability analysis).

The paper references 'Section 3.4' for scaffold-agnostic design, but the approach section ends at 3.3; minor structural errors (the running title also differs from the paper title) further indicate insufficient final-pass editing.

The retrieval stage uses a fixed top-5 with MiniLM embeddings and an LLM judge whose calibration depends on the base model; Guardian stability is only validated on GPT-4o, so behavior under GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3 (where the accept rate varies widely, 195/300 vs 286/300) is uncharacterized.

strengths: The core idea—backward reconstruction of repair reasoning plans conditioned on verified patches, injected at inference time—is well-motivated and cleanly articulated (Section 3.3, the formalization of BRD conditioning on ground-truth outcomes is clearly presented).

The evaluation covers three LLM backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3) on SWE-Bench Lite with consistent gains over the Agentless scaffold (27.3→37.7, 29.7→40.0, 27.0→35.6 Pass@1), plus statistical testing (McNemar's test).
Generalization to a second, architecturally different scaffold (mini-SWE-agent) with a comparable gain (+10.0) is a valuable robustness check that supports the scaffold-agnostic claim.

The ablation suite is reasonably thorough: Exemplar Guardian on/off, EG label stability (Agree@3 of 90%), BRD vs. MCTS-style plan generation, exemplar-vs-patch injection without a plan, and Top-1 vs. Top-3 exemplar sensitivity all isolate plausible components of the gain.

Prompt templates, the transferability rubric, the MCTS budget configuration, and data-construction details (including the ≤3-file filter and timestamp-based temporal leakage guard) are documented in appendices, aiding reproducibility.
An honest limitations section acknowledges the Python-only, SWE-Bench-Lite-only scope, dependence on repositories having suitable historical fixes, and reliance on LLM-generated judgments.
weaknesses: Figure 1 contains leftover Chinese draft annotations ('Historical dataset怎么来的？ -- issue fix dataset', '不需要分数s，迷惑', 'Stage 3 突出创新点？'), indicating the paper was not carefully proofread before submission; this undermines confidence in overall rigor.

The code-availability claim is incomplete: the abstract states 'The code is publicly available at' followed by no URL. For a paper whose central contribution is an inference-time framework, this materially weakens reproducibility.

Fairness of the headline comparisons is questionable: GPT-4o baseline numbers are taken from prior papers rather than rerun under a common harness, and the MCTS comparison uses a self-constructed, budget-fixed baseline (branching 3, 20 rollouts) that underperforms even the Agentless baseline (28.0 vs 34.0 in Table 5), making the '9.71× fewer calls / 2.47× fewer tokens' efficiency claim a comparison against a weak strawman; the authors themselves concede a matched-budget effectiveness comparison is left to future work (Appendix F).

Potential near-duplicate exemplar leakage is not adequately analyzed. SWE-Bench Lite issues within the same repository frequently have closely related sibling issues resolved earlier; the paper's temporal guard prevents leakage of the target patch itself but does not quantify how often retrieved exemplars are near-duplicates of the target fix. The Top-1/Top-3 ablation (45.0 vs 39.0 on 100 samples) hints results may be sensitive to exemplar–target proximity, but no exemplar-target similarity statistics are reported.

Several key ablations (MCTS, exemplar similarity, mini-SWE-agent) use 100-issue subsets while headline numbers use all 300, and Table 5 shows ConRAD at 41.0/45.0 on the subset vs. 37.7 on the full set, making cross-table comparisons confusing; the justification for subset choices is thin.

The method degrades to the plain scaffold for a substantial fraction of issues (195/300 exemplars accepted on GPT-4o, 257/300 on DeepSeek-V3), but the paper does not report Pass@1 separately for accepted vs. rejected exemplar issues, so it is unclear whether gains are concentrated or diffuse—important for understanding when the approach helps.

Novelty is moderate: retrospective/reverse-engineered reasoning reconstruction is acknowledged as existing (Wang et al., 2025a), and the contribution is largely an application of that idea to APR plus an LLM-judge filter and step-wise refinement; related-work positioning against retrieval-based and memory-based APR methods (which also reuse historical fixes) is asserted rather than empirically distinguished.

Presentation inconsistencies further reduce polish: the LLM-as-a-Judge prompt (Appendix C) announces 'five reasoning strategies' but lists only four; phrasing errors such as 'Ours controlled comparison analysis' and 'we only baselines where we have access' appear in Section 5; Table 5 baseline deltas are labeled inconsistently (-7.0% vs -11.0% for the same 34.0 Agentless number).

strengths: Well-motivated idea: conditioning repair reasoning backward on verified historical fixes (ConRAD) addresses a real gap—most LLM-based APR treats each issue independently, and the paper makes a clear argument for outcome-conditioned, transferable stage-wise plans as an inference-time alternative to forward search.

Comprehensive and carefully controlled evaluation: three LLM backbones (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-5) on SWE-Bench Lite with the same scaffold (Agentless), McNemar significance testing, difficulty-stratified analysis, and scaffold-generalization on mini-SWE-agent (+10.0%), supporting the claim that gains are not scaffold-specific.

Thoughtful ablations that isolate contributions: Exemplar Guardian removal (37.7→33.7 on GPT-4o), BRD vs. a controlled MCTS baseline with detailed call/token overhead accounting (Table 6), an 'Exemplar & Patch (no plan)' variant showing raw exemplar injection is insufficient, and exemplar-similarity sensitivity (Top-1 vs Top-3), including EG stability analysis (Agree@3 = 90%).

Reproducibility is strong: code is publicly released, and all key prompts (retrieval judge, Guardian rubric, distillation and refinement templates) are given in full in the appendices, along with data-construction details such as the ≤3-file patch filter and timestamp-based temporal leakage prevention.

Honest limitations section: single benchmark (Python-only), dependence on historical fix availability, and reliance on LLM-based judgments are all explicitly acknowledged, and the impact statement appropriately flags that generated patches still require validation.
weaknesses: Presentation flaw in Figure 1: the overview figure contains leftover internal editorial annotations in Chinese ('Historical dataset怎么来的? -- issue fix dataset', '不需要分数s，迷惑', 'Stage 3 突出创新点？', 'Finalization!!!'). This is careless for a submission and undermines confidence in overall polish.

Originality is moderate: retrieving similar historical fixes for APR is well established (Jiang et al. 2018, CrossFix, retrieval-based and memory-based APR), and retrospective reasoning reconstruction exists in open-ended settings (Wang et al. 2025a). The core novelty is the combination with outcome-conditioned, step-wise distillation and a conservative transferability filter—valuable but incremental relative to closely related work.

The causal mechanism behind gains is not fully explained. The 'Exemplar & Patch (no plan)' variant underperforming the no-exemplar baseline is surprising and only briefly interpreted; there is no qualitative or human analysis of what the distilled plans contain, why backward reconstruction transfers better than raw patch injection, or examples of successful vs. negative transfer. The 'globally consistent reasoning' claim remains qualitative.

Evaluation breadth is limited to SWE-Bench Lite; several baseline numbers for GPT-4o are taken from prior reports rather than rerun under identical conditions, and GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3 comparisons are mostly against the rerun Agentless scaffold only. The MCTS baseline is self-implemented with a specific budget configuration (acknowledged by the authors), so the '9.71× fewer calls' efficiency claim is a controlled ablation rather than a system-level comparison.

Some cross-referencing and consistency issues (e.g., text refers to 'Section 3.4' for scaffold-agnostic design while the approach section ends at 3.3), and the Exemplar & Patch/Top-1 ablations run on 100-sample subsets, which complicates direct comparison with the full-benchmark numbers in Table 1.

The Guardian's discrete label (Transferable/Misleading/Non-transferable) is produced by the same LLM used for repair; while stability is measured, correctness of the filter against ground-truth 'would this exemplar help' is never validated independently, leaving open whether filtering is doing what is claimed.
